Avati v Secretary, Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

27 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1597Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
No plain summary is available for this decision. Read the full text via the link below.
Key holding

Under s 19(2) of the ART Act, delay is a relevant but not automatically determinative factor in the multifactorial assessment of reasonableness, and a very long delay may set a high bar for an applicant.

The nature of the multifactorial inquiry is such that there will invariably be cases where the gravity of one factor (eg delay) will be so great and will set the bar for the applicant so high that, as a general proposition, it will be unlikely that the factual matrix will be one where it is "reasonable in all the circumstances" for the Tribunal to exercise its discretion under s 19(2).

Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

27 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1602Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationCharacter testMigration
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.
Key holding

The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

The correct identification of the limits of the primary considerations referred to in Direction 110 did not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by Mr Roseingrave.

Secretary, Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure v Thaler (No 2)

26 Oct 2026New South Wales Court of Appeal[2026] NSWCA 226Tribunal reviewVisa nomination
Before: Leeming JA; Ball JA; Price AJA at [1] Decision: 1. The Tribunal is directed, pur
The NSW Court of Appeal dealt with a notice of motion by the Secretary seeking variations to earlier orders remitting disciplinary proceedings and costs to NCAT. The Court refused to vary the remitter because its scope was already clear, but directed NCAT under cl 29(8)(d) that it may determine the remitted costs of the appeal without being satisfied of special circumstances. It otherwise dismissed the motion, with no order as to the costs of the motion.
Key holding

The Court of Appeal may, under cl 29(8)(d) of Sch 5 to the NCAT Act, direct NCAT to determine remitted costs without requiring special circumstances under s 60.

The power extends to authorising the Tribunal to depart from the rule in s 60 (which rule is explicitly displaced in a number of places in the Act: see Schedule 3 cll 12 and 13 and Schedule 5 cll 23 and 26, and Civil and Administrative Tribunal Rules 2014, rr 38 and 38A).

Bhardwaj and Commissioner of Taxation (Taxation)

23 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2482Tribunal reviewCorporations
The Tribunal reviewed a self-represented taxpayer’s objection decision concerning deductions for work-related car, travel, clothing, self-education, other expenses, gifts and tax affairs, plus interest on money borrowed to buy shares. It disallowed most deductions and held the interest was capital and not deductible, but allowed $67,500 as the third element of the cost base of the shares. The objection decision was varied accordingly.
Key holding

Interest under a bona fide loan is incurred in the income year it becomes due and payable and may be included in the third element of the cost base even if not paid.

The Tribunal expressed its view that, consistent with the established principle as expressed in Federal Commissioner of Taxation v James Flood Pty Ltd [1953] HCA 65; (1953) 88 CLR 492, the interest became due and payable in the 2020 - 21 income year and, accordingly, the balance of $67,500 was, if shown to be deductable or otherwise allowable in the cost base, deductible or allowable in its entirety in the 2020 - 21 income year.

Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

23 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1589Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.
Key holding

Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

Merhi and Tax Practitioners Board (Taxation and business)

22 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2456Tribunal reviewVisa integrityCharacter testCorporations
The Tribunal affirmed the Tax Practitioners Board’s decision to terminate Mr Merhi’s tax agent registration and impose a five-year period during which he cannot apply for registration. The decision turned on breaches of the Code of Professional Conduct and a finding that he was no longer a fit and proper person, with the Applicant’s failure to give evidence or contradict ASIC/liquidator material being significant.
Key holding

The onus of proof in establishing fitness and propriety rests with the tax practitioner. It is up to the tax practitioner to establish, and the Tribunal must be reasonably satisfied, that on the balance of probabilities and having regard to the seriousness of the matters raised that the tax practitioner or relevant individual is a fit and proper person.

Testart v Testart (No 3)

22 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1558Tribunal reviewVisa nominationEmployment & workplace
This matter concerned Ms Testart’s attempt to vacate a stay and reinstate her Fair Work proceeding after the trustee of her bankrupt estate elected under s 60(2) Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) to discontinue it; the sequestration order was later set aside. The Federal Court treated her application as one to set aside the discontinuance but refused relief because she did not challenge the trustee’s decision within the 60-day period in r 90-80 and gave no sufficient explanation for the delay.
Key holding

A party seeking a late procedural indulgence must satisfactorily explain the delay, and the Court will weigh prejudice and the administration of justice in deciding whether to grant it.

Accordingly, a party who seeks a late procedural indulgence must provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay, and the Court is entitled to consider not only prejudice to the opposing party but also the impact upon the administration of justice and the efficient use of judicial resources: Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Australian National University (2009) 239 CLR 175; UBS AG v Tyne (2018) 265 CLR 77.

Gibson and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure)

20 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2437Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
The Tribunal refused an application to appoint NDIS participant Shannon Gibson’s support coordinator, Geeta Carroll, as his litigation supporter in a Tribunal review about his NDIS plan. Although the Tribunal accepted that Mr Gibson lacked decision-making ability, it was not satisfied that the appointment was “necessary” because his representative, plan-nominee mother, interpreter, Tribunal adjustments and informal supports already allowed participation.
Key holding

Under s 67(1)(b) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth), a litigation supporter is not “necessary” merely because appointment is desirable, expedient, convenient or preferable; it is a last-resort measure required only where available and suitable other measures do not allow the party to participate.

It follows that the use of the word necessary has the effect that an appointment that would make the proceeding easier or more convenient to manage, or that the parties would welcome, is not for that reason 'necessary'. The choice of the word emphasises that an appointment is a measure of last resort, made only where the party cannot otherwise participate.

DBHP and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS)

20 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2419Tribunal reviewMigration
DBHP sought review of an NDIS statement of participant supports, challenging the refusal of various supports including support worker hours, respite, meal replacement, nutritional supplements, therapies, dietetics, occupational therapy and speech therapy. The Administrative Review Tribunal, applying s 34 of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 (Cth), affirmed the decision under review. The case is DBHP and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2419 (20 October 2026).
Key holding

Under s 34(1) of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 (Cth), all criteria are cumulative, so if any criterion is not met the support is not reasonable and necessary and cannot be funded in a statement of participant supports.

Subsection 34(1) of the NDIS Act is cumulative, meaning that all the criteria must be met. If any criteria are not met, then the requested support is not reasonable and necessary and cannot be funded under a SOPS.

Baraboutis and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS)

20 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2417Tribunal reviewMigration
Ms Baraboutis sought review of a decision refusing her access to the NDIS. The Tribunal accepted she had physical and neurological impairments and that some were permanent, but was not satisfied they caused substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c) of the NDIS Act. It affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

In assessing whether impairments result in substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c), the Tribunal must consider each specified activity as a whole rather than by reference to isolated tasks.

Further, the requirement to consider an activity as a whole, rather than by reference to tasks considered in isolation (as made plain in the amendment to s 24(1)(c)) reflects the reasoning of the Full Court of the Federal Court in National Disability Insurance Agency v Foster (2023) 295 FCR 521; [2023] FCAFC 11 ('Foster').

Lippl and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS)

20 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2416Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
This NDIS review concerned whether Ms Lippl should receive additional 1:1 support worker hours beyond those in her statement of participant supports. The Tribunal was not satisfied the requested additional hours represented value for money, finding her current flexible supports sufficient and an increase risked dependency. It nonetheless set aside and remitted the matter to fix the SoPS wording and specify support-worker assistance in accordance with the orders.
Key holding

Additional requested NDIS support worker hours are not reasonable and necessary where the evidence shows the participant can use current flexible funding to meet needs and increased hours risk dependency, so the value-for-money criterion is not met.

The Tribunal has determined the requested additional support worker hours do not satisfy the statutory requirement of representing value for money and cannot be approved by the Tribunal. The evidence is that Ms Lippl can use her support worker hours flexibly, that the current provision is sufficient to meet her needs and that increasing her hours risks creating dependency on support workers over time.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson

20 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1548Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.
Key holding

Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

Hoang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration)

19 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2396Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
The Tribunal reviewed the Minister’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Hoang’s Class BF Transitional (Permanent) visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although Mr Hoang had a substantial criminal record for repeat drug and weapons offending and failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4) and set aside the refusal.
Key holding

A residual risk of reoffending may be acceptable, and another reason to revoke may exist, where serious addiction-related offending is offset by sustained rehabilitation, family support and long residence.

The Applicant has, nonetheless, made significant progress in rehabilitation and has retained the support and trust of his immediate family who are an important element to his future success. RSZN v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

The Federal Court judicially reviewed an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming the refusal of a Safe Haven Enterprise (subclass 790) visa to an Iraqi former army officer. It is not sufficient that the accessory merely knows that his or her conduct will assist the principal perpetrator in the commission of the offence.

Key holding

A protection visa may be granted on complementary protection grounds where the refugee criterion is not met, if removal creates a real risk of significant harm as a necessary and foreseeable consequence.

The issues in this case are whether the applicants have a well-founded fear of being persecuted in India for one or more of the five reasons set out, and, if not, whether there are substantial grounds for believing that, as a necessary and foreseeable consequence of the applicant being removed from Australia to India there is a real risk that they will suffer significant harm.

In Yerburgh and Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] ARTA 2291, the Tribunal reviewed a decision reducing Mrs Yerburgh’s age pension by assessing notional income from a farm treated as an unrealisable asset. Key holding

However, having heard from Mrs Yerburgh, the Tribunal is satisfied that the farm is currently being operated commercially to its full capacity. As such, the Tribunal finds that what Mrs Yerburgh could reasonably be expected to obtain from a purely commercial application of the farm is the income that is actually being generated from its current operations, not some alternative higher commercial lease figure as adopted by Centrelink.

Key holding

For discretionary waiver under s 101, special circumstances require the individual circumstances to be outside the usual or ordinary course; mere inadvertence, financial hardship or administrative delay will not suffice.

Special circumstances' is not a term defined in the legislation. Key holding

PIC 4020 is engaged where there is an element of fraud or deception by some person, although the applicant need not have known that the information was purposely untrue.

While PIC 4020 refers to information that is false, in the sense of purposely untrue, it is not necessary for the Minister (or the Tribunal on review) to conclude that the applicant was aware the information was purposely untrue in order for PIC 4020 to be engaged. However, an element of fraud or deception by some person is necessary to attract the operation of the provision: Trivedi v MIBP [2014] FCAFC 42.

The Tribunal (ARTA) affirmed the refusal of a protection visa to a Tongan national who arrived in Australia as a minor and feared homelessness/economic hardship in Tonga due to having no family or support network. Key holding

Economic hardship or lack of support does not amount to persecution or significant harm unless an entity in the receiving country would cause that harm.

Each of the verbal phrases contained in the categories of harm which form the definition of 'significant harm' contemplate that there is an entity in the country concerned which would cause that harm; that is, 'will be arbitrarily deprived of', 'will be carried out on', and 'will be subjected to'. Because there is no entity which would seek to cause any of those categories of harm to the Applicant, he does not meet the statutory criterion for complementary protection.

This is a Tribunal review of a delegate’s refusal of protection visas to a Malaysian husband and wife. The first applicant claimed harm arising from opposition to land acquisition and a proposed chemical factory, but the Tribunal found his claims lacked detail, were inconsistent and were not credible, and affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

Applicants bear responsibility for providing sufficient particulars and supporting evidence, and mere assertions of feared harm do not themselves establish a well-founded fear or real risk of significant harm.

It is well established that the mere assertions by an applicant that he or she fears persecution for particular reasons, such assertions do not of themselves establish the validity of the asserted fears, for the reasons claimed or that such fears are well-founded. Similarly, such claims, that an applicant faces a real risk of significant harm do not of themselves establish that these risks exist or amount to a 'real risk' or significant harm.

Mdallal (Migration)

18 May 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2382Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
This was a review of a delegate’s decision to cancel Mr Mdallal’s Subclass 820 (Spouse) visa after he was convicted of contravening an AVO and common assault. Although the Tribunal found the conviction ground for cancellation was made out, it exercised the discretion not to cancel because of his remarriage, his support for two minor children (including an autistic stepdaughter), and the hardship removal would cause. The Tribunal set aside the cancellation and substituted a decision not to cancel.
Key holding

Even where a conviction ground for cancellation under s 116(1)(g) is established, the Tribunal may decline to cancel a temporary spouse visa where the best interests of affected children and associated family hardship outweigh the seriousness of the offending in the particular circumstances.

In the particular circumstances of this case, the Tribunal has decided to give greatest weight to the best interests of the children which weigh against the cancellation. Considering the circumstances as a whole, the Tribunal concludes that the cancellation should be set aside.

Pillay v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCAFC 24 (19 March 2026)

19 Mar 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 24Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationCharacter test
The Full Court considered an appeal from judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming non-revocation of Mr Pillay’s visa cancellation under the Migration Act. The Tribunal’s adverse credit findings relied on an allegedly wrong premise that Mr Pillay had withheld documents from a psychologist, and it also declined to give weight to Australian business interests under Direction 99. The Full Court allowed the appeal, quashed the Tribunal decision and remitted the review.
Key holding

A tribunal may commit jurisdictional error by constructively failing to review if it fails to make an obvious inquiry into a critical fact that is easily ascertained and that failure has a sufficient link to the outcome.

It may be that a failure to make an obvious inquiry about a critical fact, the existence of which is easily ascertained, could, in some circumstances, supply a sufficient link to the outcome to constitute a failure to review. If so, such a failure could give rise to jurisdictional error by constructive failure to exercise jurisdiction.

Sharma v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 269 (17 March 2026)

17 Mar 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 269Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Mr Sharma sought a Regional Sponsored Migration Scheme (subclass 187) visa based on a nomination by Shivram Australia Pty Ltd. The nomination was refused/withdrawn, so the Tribunal affirmed the visa refusal because cl 187.233(3) required an approved nomination, and the Federal Circuit and Family Court dismissed judicial review. On appeal to the Federal Court, Mr Sharma alleged the Tribunal and primary judge failed to engage with his claims that he was defrauded by the nominator and denied natural justice.
Key holding

Third-party fraud does not amount to jurisdictional error unless it stultifies or otherwise affects the decision-maker’s exercise of statutory power; the mandatory approved-nomination criterion remains determinative.

There was no such approved nomination application at the time that the Minister and thereafter the Tribunal considered Mr Sharma's application. Accordingly, whatever the alleged fraud may have been that occurred before the nomination application was refused and the circumstances in which the nominator's review application was withdrawn, that alleged fraud did not affect the Tribunal's, and thereafter the FCFCOA's, power to carry out their respective statutory tasks.

HLWS v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 243 (12 March 2026)

12 Mar 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 243Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewCharacter test
HLWS sought an extension of time and judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Resolution of Status visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal accepted a psychologist’s low/moderate reoffending risk assessed “without intervention” but did not address HLWS’s willingness to undertake interventions. The Federal Court granted the extension and allowed review, finding a material jurisdictional error.
Key holding

A tribunal commits jurisdictional error where it overlooks a substantial and clearly articulated contention that is material to its statutory risk assessment, such that the outcome could realistically have been different.

Accordingly, in my view, in failing to consider the interventions point at all, the Tribunal failed to discharge the task and function accorded to it by Parliament, and engaged in jurisdictional error.

Sam Abdi v Heart Of Melbourne Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 810 (12 March 2026)

12 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 810Employment & workplaceTribunal reviewVisa nomination
Mr Abdi applied under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy against Heart Of Melbourne Pty Ltd. He failed to file material as directed and did not attend a compliance hearing. The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application for want of prosecution.
Key holding

Under s.587(1), the FWC may dismiss an application on its own initiative where the applicant unreasonably fails to comply with directions and attend hearings, effectively abandoning prosecution, though the power is exercised with caution.

As noted above, s.587(1) does not limit when the Commission may dismiss an application. Mr Abdi has, in effect, abandoned his application and it is not appropriate that the Respondent be subject to further proceedings or costs in this matter.

San Bao Pty Ltd v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] HCA 6 (11 March 2026)

11 Mar 2026High Court of Australia[2026] HCA 6Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal review
San Bao Pty Ltd sought constitutional writs of certiorari and mandamus in the High Court after a delegate refused its nomination of Ms Haiming Du for a Subclass 482 (Skills in Demand) visa, the Company having missed the 28-day ART review period. The Company alleged the delegate constructively failed to exercise jurisdiction or acted unreasonably by refusing the nomination on the supposed basis that no organisational chart or staffing-structure evidence had been provided.
Key holding

A decision-maker’s reasons must be read as a whole and in context; a reference to an absent organisational chart does not establish that the decision-maker mistakenly believed no chart was provided where the actual concern was insufficient evidence of how the nominated role fitted the staffing structure.

When the references by the delegate in their reasons to an "organisation[al] chart" are properly understood in their context, it can be seen that the delegate was concerned with the absence of sufficient evidence, including from an organisational chart, that explained the need for an additional cook by detailing the relationship that the additional cook would have within the existing structure.

RE AFRICAN GOLD LTD; EX PARTE AFRICAN GOLD LTD [2026] WASC 61 (10 March 2026)

10 Mar 2026Supreme Court of Western Australia[2026] WASC 61Tribunal reviewVisa cancellation
African Gold Ltd sought orders under s 411(1) of the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) to convene meetings of its shareholders and optionholders to consider two inter-conditional schemes of arrangement with Montage Gold Corp. Under the schemes, Montage would acquire all African Gold shares and all outstanding options would be cancelled and exchanged for new Montage options, with African Gold becoming a wholly-owned Montage subsidiary and delisting from ASX.
Key holding

On a first court hearing under s 411(1), the Court will convene scheme meetings where the statutory and procedural requirements are satisfied and the proposed arrangement is fit for consideration by members, judged by whether sensible businesspeople might consider it beneficial.

If the proposed arrangement is one that appears fit for consideration by a meeting of members and is a commercial proposition likely to gain the court's approval if passed by the necessary majority, leave should be given to convene the meeting.

Michales v CharterLaw Legal Pty Limited [2026] FCA 209 (6 March 2026)

6 Mar 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 209Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal review
Mr Michales sought review of a Registrar’s decision refusing to set aside bankruptcy notice BN279414, issued on CharterLaw Legal Pty Ltd’s application for unpaid legal fees totalling $107,654.53. He argued CLL could not recover or enforce the debt because it had ceased legal practice on 30 June 2024 and was not a qualified entity under the Legal Profession Uniform Law (NSW). Perry J dismissed the application, refused amendment/subpoena/notice to produce relief, and upheld the bankruptcy notice.
Key holding

A company that provided legal services while licensed does not contravene s 10(1) of the LPUL merely by suing on its own behalf to recover unpaid fees after ceasing practice.

By commencing proceedings on its own behalf to recover a debt from the applicant, CLL does not engage in legal practice.

eSafety Commissioner v Baumgarten [2026] FCAFC 12 (18 February 2026)

18 Feb 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 12Migration: court challengeTribunal review
The Full Court dismissed the eSafety Commissioner’s appeal from the Administrative Review Tribunal, which had found it had jurisdiction to review a “complaint alert” sent to X about Ms Baumgarten’s post. The Tribunal treated the alert as a decision in fact to give a removal notice under s 88 of the Online Safety Act 2021 (Cth), even though the Commissioner said it was informal and not legally effective. The Full Court upheld that approach and the appeal was dismissed with no costs.
Key holding

For Tribunal review jurisdiction, a decision in fact to give a notice is reviewable as a s 88 removal notice if its objective features amount to such a notice, regardless of the decision-maker’s subjective intention or the notice’s legal effectiveness.

All that is required is that a decision to give a notice of some kind was made, and that, having regard to its objective features, the notice that was given amounts, as a matter of fact, to a removal notice as described in s 88(1).

Spaleta v Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] FCAFC 5 (11 February 2026)

11 Feb 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 5Tribunal reviewVisa nomination
This was a Full Court appeal about a disability support pension claim. The appellant challenged the AAT’s finding that her conditions were not fully treated or stabilised, so she could not get 20 impairment points under s 94(1)(b) of the Social Security Act 1991 (Cth). The Full Court allowed the appeal, holding that “reasonable treatment” under the Impairment Tables Determination requires consideration of whether treatment is affordable to the claimant, and remitted the matter.
Key holding

In assessing whether treatment is “reasonable treatment” under s 6(7) of the Impairment Tables Determination, “reasonable cost” requires consideration of whether the treatment is reasonably affordable to the claimant in their circumstances, not merely whether the cost is objectively reasonable in the market.

A question arises as to whether the reference to "reasonable cost" in s 6(7)(b) is to the objective reasonableness of the cost of the treatment, or to the different question whether the treatment is reasonably affordable to a claimant in the position of the person concerned. In our view, the latter is the better construction having regard to the context and purpose of the provision.

September 2025 (1)

2114521 (Refugee)

16 Sep 2025Administrative Review Tribunal[2025] ARTA 3466Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a subclass 866 protection visa to a Chinese national who claimed persecution arising from a family shop/land dispute involving local government, a developer and his father’s petitioning. At hearing, the applicant contradicted those written claims, said he did not fear harm on return to China, and explained he wished to stay in Australia for work and family financial reasons. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

An applicant for a protection visa bears the responsibility to establish all statutory elements by sufficient evidence, and the Tribunal is not required to make the applicant’s case.

It remains for the applicant to satisfy the Tribunal that all of the statutory elements are established. A decision-maker is not required to make the applicant's case for him or her.

October 2024 (124)

2002567 (Refugee)

11 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4218Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Don Smyth
This was an AATA review of a delegate’s refusal of a protection visa to an applicant who claimed South African citizenship but was born and lived in Zimbabwe. He claimed fear in South Africa and/or Zimbabwe as a gay, mixed-race/“coloured” man, a political opponent of Zanu-PF, and because of economic conditions and crime. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

For complementary protection, a real risk is not established where the risk is one faced by the population generally and not personally by the applicant.

Under s 36(2B)(c) of the Act there is taken not to be a real risk that an applicant will suffer significant harm if the Tribunal is satisfied that the real risk is one faced by the population generally and is not faced by the applicant personally.

2016849 (Refugee)

11 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4209Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Lilly Mojsin
This was an Administrative Review Tribunal (Migration & Refugee Division) review of a delegate’s refusal to grant protection visas to Chinese applicants who claimed harm from loan sharks, debt collectors, gangdom and police in China. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal because the applicants consented to a decision on the papers and the Tribunal was not satisfied their claims were made out or that they faced a real chance or real risk of harm on return to China.
Key holding

A protection visa applicant bears the onus of establishing all statutory elements; mere assertions of feared persecution or significant harm are insufficient unless they satisfy the Tribunal that a well-founded fear or real risk exists.

The mere fact that a person claims fear of persecution for a particular reason does not establish either the genuineness of the asserted fear or that it is "well-founded" or that it is for the reason claimed. Similarly, that the applicant claims to face a real risk of significant harm does not establish that such a risk exists, or that the harm feared amounts to "significant harm".

1919845 (Refugee)

10 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4472Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Rupert Timms
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a protection visa to a Vietnamese Kinh Buddhist man who claimed fear of harm in Vietnam arising from low-level protest activity in Australia. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal because the evidence did not establish a well-founded fear of persecution or a real risk of significant harm. It also found no jurisdiction over the son’s review because the son had become an Australian citizen, but referred the father’s case to the Minister under s 417.
Key holding

Conduct engaged in by a protection visa applicant in Australia must be disregarded in assessing well-founded fear unless the applicant proves it was not done to strengthen the refugee claim.

In determining whether the person has a well‑founded fear of persecution for one or more of the reasons mentioned in paragraph (1)(a), any conduct engaged in by the person in Australia is to be disregarded unless the person satisfies the Minister that the person engaged in the conduct otherwise than for the purpose of strengthening the person's claim to be a refugee.

1913055 (Refugee)

10 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4462Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Raymond Smith
This is a Malaysian citizen’s application for review of a delegate’s refusal to grant a protection visa. The applicant claimed economic hardship and unspecified difficulties in Malaysia but declined a Tribunal hearing and provided no further evidence. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal because it was not satisfied she faced a well-founded fear of persecution or a real risk of significant harm.
Key holding

An applicant for a protection visa bears the responsibility to specify all particulars of the claim and provide sufficient evidence; the Tribunal is not required to make the applicant's case or accept uncritically mere assertions.

It remains for the applicant to satisfy the Tribunal that all of the statutory elements are made out. A decision-maker is not required to make the applicant's case for him or her.

1917587 (Refugee)

10 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4461Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Frank Russo
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal of protection visas for a Thai family who claimed they feared harm in Thailand from a money lender associated with organised crime over unpaid agricultural debts. The Tribunal accepted the applicants’ identity and nationality but made adverse credibility findings and found no well-founded fear of persecution or real risk of significant harm. It affirmed the delegate’s refusal.
Key holding

A claimed fear of persecution is not well-founded unless supported by credible, non-speculative evidence; the Tribunal may reject uncritical assertions and find the claimed fear not established.

The Tribunal notes that the mere fact that a person claims fear of persecution for a particular reason does not establish the genuineness of the asserted fear, that the fear is "well-founded" or that it is for the reason claimed. A fear of persecution is not "well-founded" if it is merely assumed or if it is mere speculation.

The further review application lodged on 27 June 2024 was therefore invalid.
Key holding

Once the Tribunal has validly reviewed a reviewable decision and completed its statutory review, that decision ceases to be reviewable and the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction to review the same delegate decision again.

Where the Tribunal has received a valid application for review of a reviewable decision and carried out its statutory duty to review the decision under the Act, the decision is no longer a reviewable decision: SZBWJ v MIAC [2008] FMCA 164 at [41] and the cases cited therein. The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to review a delegate's decision twice: Jayasinghe v MIEA (1997) 76 FCR 301 and SZASP v MIAC [2007] FCA 771.

The Tribunal affirmed the refusal but referred his circumstances to the Minister under s 351.
Key holding

For the long residence applicant definition, time spent physically outside the migration zone as a minor is not constructively treated as time in the migration zone.

The Tribunal is not persuaded, despite the considerable efforts of the representative, that it can reasonably interpret travel overseas as a minor as constructively being time 'in the migration zone' for the purposes of an applicant being eligible to be a long residence applicant for a Former Resident visa.

2115044 (Refugee)

24 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3976Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Sue Zelinka
The applicant, a Macedonian citizen, sought review of a refusal of a protection visa based on feared harm from family and an alleged criminal gang after his secret marriage to his first cousin became known. It affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

A particular social group claim cannot succeed where the asserted group is not cognisable because its defining marriage is unlawful in the receiving country, or where the group is defined only by a shared fear of persecution or family harm.

The Tribunal rejects this formulation noting that there is no such group because first cousins, by law, cannot marry in Macedonia and therefore there cannot be a large, cognisable group of them. Any other variation of particular social group involving victims of harm at family hands is also rejected because a particular social group cannot be constituted by persons bound only by fear of persecution.

Cai (Migration)

23 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3835Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Paul Windsor
Mr Cai applied for a Visitor (Class FA) subclass 600 visa in the Tourist stream. The delegate refused the visa because it was not satisfied he genuinely intended to stay temporarily in Australia under cl 600.211. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding his long continuous stay and unsupported medical claims indicated he was using the visitor visa to establish de facto residence.
Key holding

To satisfy cl 600.211, the applicant must positively satisfy the Tribunal of a genuine intention to stay temporarily for the visa purpose; a long continuous stay without a credible departure timeframe or supporting medical evidence can show the visitor visa is being used for de facto residence.

Given the applicant has been in Australia continuously since January 2020 and could not give any time-frame within which he might feel well enough to depart Australia, the Tribunal considers the applicant is seeking to use the subclass 600 Visitor visa to establish de facto residence in Australia. Consequently, the Tribunal is not satisfied that the visa applicant genuinely intends to stay temporarily in Australia for the purpose for which the visa would be granted.

Mohamed and Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs (Migration)

10 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3606Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationMigration
Mr Mohamed sought review of a delegate’s refusal of his Partner Visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the refusal notice was emailed to his nominated address on 18 June 2024 and deemed received that day, so his 26 August 2024 review application was about two months outside the mandatory nine-day period in s 500(6B). It held it had no jurisdiction and dismissed the application under s 42A(4) of the Administrative Appeals Tribunal Act 1975 (Cth).
Key holding

A s 501G notice sent by email to the recipient’s designated address is taken to be received at the end of the day of transmission, commencing the nine-day review period under s 500(6B).

He was therefore taken to have received it by the end of that day. The nine-day time limit for an appeal then began to run and Mr Mohamed had until 27 June 2024 to lodge his review application but did not do so until 26 August 2024, approximately two months later.

The Hour Glass (Australia) Pty Ltd sought review of a delegate’s refusal to approve a nomination for a Subclass 482 visa in the Short-term stream. Alvindo (Migration)

9 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3378Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationMigration
Before: David McCulloch
Alvindo concerns review of a delegate’s decision to cancel Mr Alvindo’s Subclass 500 (Student) visa after he was convicted of knowingly possessing child abuse material and two optical surveillance device offences. The Tribunal found the conviction ground was made out but affirmed cancellation after weighing the serious privacy offences against his study record, remorse and hardship. It is a discretionary migration cancellation decision.
Key holding

A conviction for an offence against a Commonwealth, State or Territory law is a prescribed ground for cancellation under s 116(1)(g), and where s 116(3) does not mandate cancellation the Tribunal must exercise the cancellation discretion.

For these reasons, the Tribunal is satisfied that the ground for cancellation in s 116(1)(g) exists. As that ground does not require mandatory cancellation under s 116(3), the Tribunal must proceed to consider whether the visa should be cancelled.

9 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3264Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
The applicant, a UK-born minor, applied for Australian citizenship by descent through his mother, an Australian citizen by descent. A delegate refused the application because the mother had not been present in Australia for the required two years (730 days) before the application. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding no discretion to overcome the shortfall.
Key holding

Under s 16(2)(b)(i) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), the two-year presence requirement is mandatory and the Minister or Tribunal has no discretion to approve citizenship by descent if it is not met.

There is no discretion available to the Minister with respect to an Applicant not meeting the requirements of section 16(2) of the Act. If these prescriptive legislative requirements are not able to be met, the citizenship application cannot be approved.

Michael Hughes, a 58-year-old New Zealand/United Kingdom citizen, had his subclass 189 visa mandatorily cancelled after being convicted of indecent dealing with a child under 13 and sentenced to 20 months’ imprisonment. Key holding

In those circumstances, it is not open to the Tribunal to go behind the essential facts of that conviction and sentence. Moreover, the Applicant has not discharged what would otherwise be his "heavy onus" to challenge the facts upon which the conviction and sentence are necessarily based as set out above.

1829009 (Refugee)

29 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3962Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewVisa integrityMigration
Before: Maralean McCalman
This was an AATA review of a delegate’s refusal to grant a protection visa to a Malaysian citizen of Kadazan ethnicity and Christian faith. The applicant claimed employment discrimination, limited opportunities and poverty in Sabah; the Tribunal accepted some discrimination but found the harm did not meet the protection thresholds. It affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

Employment discrimination causing only relative economic disadvantage, without serious harm as defined in s 5J(5), does not establish a well-founded fear of persecution.

Thus, the Tribunal finds that the level of harm the applicant will experience does not rise to the level of constituting serious harm as outlined in s 5J(5) of the Act.

2210099 (Refugee)

29 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3931Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Fraser Robertson
This is an AATA review of a delegate’s refusal to grant protection visas to a married Macedonian couple. They claimed to fear harm from a March 2018 armed attack allegedly linked to Applicant 1’s brief service in the 2001 Macedonian conflict, plus Applicant 2’s mental health and work capacity. The Tribunal accepted some background but rejected the claimed attack as implausible and affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

A decision-maker assessing complementary protection may rely on relevant findings made in the refugee assessment where the factual bases overlap.

To the extent that the factual bases for claims under s 36(2)(a) and s 36(2)(aa) overlap, a decision-maker, when considering the complementary protection criterion under s 36(2)(aa), is entitled to refer to and rely on any relevant findings the decision-maker made when considering the refugee criterion under s 36(2)(a).

1911439 (Refugee)

29 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3613Tribunal reviewMigration
Before: Alison Ryan
This is a review of a delegate’s refusal of a protection visa to an applicant from China. The applicant failed to attend the scheduled Tribunal hearing, and after the Tribunal dismissed the application, did not seek reinstatement within 14 days. The Tribunal confirmed the dismissal.
Key holding

Where an applicant fails to attend a scheduled Tribunal hearing and does not apply for reinstatement within 14 days of receiving the dismissal statement, the Tribunal must confirm the dismissal and the decision under review is taken to be affirmed.

As the applicant did not apply for reinstatement of the application within the 14 days period, the Tribunal must confirm the decision to dismiss the application. In these circumstances, the decision under review is taken to be affirmed.

Latu (Migration)

29 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3132Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Meena Sripathy
The Tribunal affirmed the refusal of a Child (Residence) (Class BT) visa (Subclass 802) to an applicant who was 18 at the time of application. The sponsor stepfather held Family Law Act sole parental responsibility orders after the applicant’s mother died, but there was no adoption and the Tribunal found the migration criteria were not met. The Tribunal nevertheless referred the matter for Ministerial intervention based on compelling family circumstances.
Key holding

An applicant over 18 at the time of application cannot satisfy the r 1.03 step-child definition for a Subclass 802 visa where reliance is placed on being the child of a former spouse/de facto partner, even if the sponsor holds a Family Law Act sole parental responsibility order.

He was 18 years at the time of application, therefore he does not meet the requirements of the definition of step child in subparagraph (b) of the definition in r.1.03, despite the Family Law Act 1975 court order dated 24 February 2020 which gave the sponsor sole parental responsibility for him.

2411479 (Refugee)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3799Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Peter Katsambanis
The Tribunal found it had no jurisdiction to review a refusal of a protection visa because the review application was lodged late. The delegate refused the visa on 6 April 2024, but the applicant did not lodge her review until 10 May 2024, outside the 28-day period.
Key holding

For a protection visa review where the applicant is not in immigration detention, the application must be lodged within 28 days starting on the day of notification; if lodged late, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction.

As the applicant was not in immigration detention on the day the applicant was notified of the decision, an application for review of the decision had to be made within 28 days, commencing on that day: reg 4.31(2) of the Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth) (the Regulations).

Barik (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3417Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Sheridan Aster
The Tribunal considered an application to review a refusal to grant a Training (Class GF) Subclass 407 visa. Because the associated nomination had been refused and the applicant was not nominated by an approved sponsor at the time of the review application, the Tribunal found the visa refusal was not a reviewable decision. The application was therefore dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Key holding

A refusal of a Training (Subclass 407) visa is reviewable only if, at the time of the review application, the applicant has an approved sponsor nomination or has a pending review of the nomination refusal.

A decision to refuse a Training visa is reviewable if the applicant made the visa application while in the migration zone and the applicant is nominated by an approved sponsor at the time the application for review of the visa refusal is made or an application for review of a decision not to approve the nomination has been made but at the time the application for review of the visa refusal is made, review of the decision is pending.

Gowing Advisory Chartered Accountants (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3416Tribunal reviewVisa nominationMigration
Before: Rosa Gagliardi
Gowing Advisory Chartered Accountants sought Tribunal review of a delegate's refusal of a Standard Business Nomination. The Tribunal found it had no jurisdiction because the applicant did not pay the full prescribed review fee within the prescribed period. The applicant had paid part of the fee but declined to pay the balance and sought a refund.
Key holding

A migration review application is not valid, and the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction, where the prescribed fee has not been paid within the prescribed period or any applicable reasonable period after a hardship-reduction determination.

The Tribunal considers the applicant has been given a reasonable period to pay the fee since being notified of the authorised officer's decision; however, the fee has not been paid. The application for review is therefore not a valid application and the Tribunal has no jurisdiction in this matter.

Goncalves De Sa (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3350Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
Before: Peter Emmerton
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of Employer Nomination (Permanent) (Class EN) Subclass 186 visas in the Temporary Residence Transition stream because the primary applicant, a chef, could not demonstrate competent English at the time of application. Although he spoke English well at hearing and had substantial culinary experience, his IELTS results and Portuguese passport did not meet the prescribed criteria, and the Tribunal had no discretion.
Key holding

For a Subclass 186 TRT visa, competent English must be established at the time of application through a specified test score or specified passport, failing which cl 186.222(a) is not satisfied and the Tribunal has no discretion.

Since neither 1.15C(1) nor 1.15C(2) are satisfied, 1.15C is not satisfied. As 1.15C is not satisfied, the Tribunal finds the applicant did not have competent English at the time of lodging the visa application, and therefore does not satisfy 186.222(a).

Jiang (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3198Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Tania Flood
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of Ms Jiang’s Visitor (Class FA) Subclass 600 visa because she applied after her substantive visa expired. It found the late application resulted from forgetfulness and inadequate reminders, not factors beyond her control under Schedule 3 criterion 3004(c). The applicant was also offshore at the time of decision, so cl 600.411 was not met.
Key holding

Under criterion 3004(c), whether the applicant ceased to hold a substantive visa because of factors beyond their control is assessed subjectively and practically, and forgetfulness or failure to take available compliance measures will not ordinarily qualify.

The test is in that sense "subjective" rather than being directed at deciding what would have been beyond the control of an abstract or "reasonable" person. A second point is that what is "beyond control" should be tested by considering whether the happening of the event was or was not within the control of the applicant in a practical or realistic sense.

2411742 (Refugee)

27 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4375Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewVisa integrityMigration
Before: Damian Creedon
The applicant is an older South Korean citizen who claimed protection in Australia because he feared being unable to find work in South Korea due to age discrimination and long absence. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal of his protection visa, finding South Korea offers effective protection against age discrimination and that his economic/employment concerns did not meet protection criteria.
Key holding

Effective protection measures available from the receiving State can negate a well-founded fear of persecution under s 5J(2).

The Tribunal finds, therefore, that South Korea can offer effective protection to its citizens against age discrimination. It follows, and the Tribunal finds, that effective protection measures against age discrimination are available to the applicant in South Korea, and that therefore he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution on that ground: s 5J(2).

Sio and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (Migration)

10 Jan 2023Administrative Review Tribunal[2023] AATA 9Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationCharacter testMigration
Mr Sio, a New Zealand citizen holding a subclass 444 visa, had his visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) and a delegate decided not to revoke the cancellation under s 501CA(4). Following the Full Federal Court's decision in Pearson, the cancellation was invalid because an aggregate sentence is not a term of imprisonment of 12 months or more, so the visa was taken not to have been cancelled and the revocation decision was a nullity. The Tribunal held it had no jurisdiction to review the nullity and dismissed the application by consent.
